title: Packet-Syscall Coordinated Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Network Stack
authors: Guoyu Yin; Yuhan Chen; Changjian Liu; Weibo Zhang; Fan Ding; Dalong Shi; Yuheng Shen; Heyuan Shi
abstract: The Linux kernel network stack is a safety-critical subsystem that manages network communications, such as TCP/IP session handling and UDP datagram routing. However, effectively fuzzing the kernel network stack presents significant challenges: large portions of code are disabled by static configurations; generating network-specific inputs for both syscalls and packets is difficult; and testing the interplay between syscall execution and packet injection requires precise coordination. In this paper, we introduce Pacaller, a packet-syscall coordinated fuzzer designed for the kernel network stack. Pacaller first performs automated configuration analysis to enhance code reachability. Then, Pacaller extracts network resources from the kernel source code to generate network-specific syscall specifications and packet models. Finally, Pacaller coordinates syscall execution with packet injection to test their complex interactions within the network stack. We implemented and evaluated Pacaller on four recent versions of the Linux kernel, discovering 26 previously unknown bugs (16 confirmed, 10 fixed). Pacaller also achieved 13.3% to 22.3% higher network stack coverage than Syzkaller, SyzGen++, KernelGPT, Syz-TCP, and TRON. These results demonstrate that Pacaller significantly improves the effectiveness of fuzzing the kernel network stack.

title: Hybrid Fuzzing with LLM-Guided Input Mutation and Semantic Feedback
authors: Shiyin Lin
abstract: Software fuzzing has become a cornerstone in automated vulnerability discovery, yet existing mutation strategies often lack semantic awareness, leading to redundant test cases and slow exploration of deep program states. In this work, we present a hybrid fuzzing framework that integrates static and dynamic analysis with Large Language Model (LLM)-guided input mutation and semantic feedback. Static analysis extracts control-flow and data-flow information, which is transformed into structured prompts for the LLM to generate syntactically valid and semantically diverse inputs. During execution, we augment traditional coverage-based feedback with semantic feedback signals—derived from program state changes, exception types, and output semantics—allowing the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that trigger novel program behaviors beyond mere code coverage. We implement our approach atop AFL++, combining program instrumentation with embedding-based semantic similarity metrics to guide seed selection. Evaluation on real-world open-source targets, including libpng, tcpdump, and sqlite, demonstrates that our method achieves faster time-to-first-bug, higher semantic diversity, and a competitive number of unique bugs compared to state-of-the-art fuzzers. This work highlights the potential of combining LLM reasoning with semantic-aware feedback to accelerate and deepen vulnerability discovery.

title: Virtualization-Backed Kernel Fuzzing with Crash-Resilient Snapshot Orchestration Authors
authors: Claire Dupont; Julien Moreau; Émile Laurent
abstract: Kernel fuzzing often suffers from unstable system states and long reboot cycles after a crash. In this study, we introduce a virtualization-backed fuzzing framework using differential snapshot orchestration. Each fuzzing iteration restores from a minimal kernel state snapshot with deterministic I/O replay. On KVM and Firecracker, our technique reduces per-crash recovery latency from 1.8 seconds to 220 ms, improving overall fuzzing throughput by 3.7×. It discovers 16 bugs, including memory leaks, lock mismanagement, and two high-severity kernel panics. The approach provides a stable, reproducible environment for large-scale kernel fuzzing activities.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Input Scheduling for Kernel Fuzzing Authors
authors: Javier Ruiz; Laura Fernández; María González
abstract: In this study, we propose an RL-guided fuzzing scheduler that learns optimal mutation ordering and seed prioritization based on kernel coverage reward signals. The agent observes execution depth, subsystem transitions, and historical crash density to adapt exploration strategies. On Linux 5.10, the RL-fuzzer triggers 22% more unique crashes and 31% more deep paths compared with AFL-style schedulers. It identifies 7 previously unknown vulnerabilities, including mismanaged capability checks. Despite additional overhead from RL inference, throughput remains within 85% of baseline fuzzers. This study demonstrates the feasibility of applying RL-based policy learning to kernel fuzzing orchestration.

title: Does the Verdict Function Matter? How Evaluation Rewards Causally Steer Automated LLM Fuzzing and Distort Discovered Vulnerabilities
authors: Ashish Vishwakarma
abstract: When security teams run automated red-teaming fuzzers against Large Language Models (LLMs), an automated verdict function acts as the reward signal guiding the search algorithm. While recent studies have examined static differences between scoring metrics, an essential question remains unaddressed: How does the choice of verdict function causally steer what an active adversarial search algorithm discovers and misses? In this paper, we run a controlled experiment showing that the verdict function acts as an active steering wheel rather than a passive scoreboard. Holding the target model (Qwen2-57B-A14B-Instruct), the search algorithm (UCB-1 bandit fuzzer), the mutation operators, and query budgets strictly invariant, we evaluate five canonical verdict functions: refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), keyword blocklists (𝑉 2), LLM-as-a-judge (𝑉 3), lexical intent preservation (𝑉 4), and multi-objective combined scoring (𝑉 5). Our investigation establishes four primary findings: (1) Causal Search Steering &amp; Policy Collapse (Headline Finding): When guided by refusal-prefix matching (𝑉 1), the multi-armed bandit fuzzer rapidly collapses into selecting superficial conversational wrappers (38.6%). The set of successful jailbreak prompts discovered under 𝑉 1 shares only a 12.0% Jaccard overlap (𝐽 = 0.120) with those discovered under multi-objective guidance (𝑉 5). (2) Search Blindness to Real Vulnerabilities: Because prefix matching rewards non-refusal conversational fillers, the fuzzer spends its query budget harvesting superficial text (𝜇 = 1.42/5.0 relevance), remaining systematically blind to over 85% of the actionable jailbreak vectors discovered under semantic guidance. (3) Massive Reporting Divergence (Δ &gt; 50%): On identical model responses from Qwen2-57B, prefix matching reports an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.2%, compared to 31.8% under combined evaluation (𝑝 = 1.83 × 10-10 under McNemar's test). (4) Downstream Defense Contamination: Defensive activation probes trained on hard negatives mined under prefix matching suffer a 0.208 drop in test AUROC (AUROC = 0.786 vs. 0.991) because labeling errors pollute defensive training boundaries. We establish the Calibrated Dual-Verdict Protocol (CDVP) to prevent metric-induced search distortion and ensure reliable vulnerability discovery in automated red-teaming. title: Constraint-Informed Directed Kernel Fuzzing for Hard-to-Reach Code Regions Authors
authors: Giulia Romano; Luca Ferraro; Marco Bianchi
abstract: In this study, we explore constraint inference to improve directed fuzzing for rarely executed kernel regions. The proposed system extracts partial symbolic constraints using lightweight solver queries and integrates them with distance-based fuzzing heuristics. Testing on 10 common Linux drivers, the fuzzer reduces target-reaching time by 63% and uncovers 6 new memory-corruption issues. Constraint caching avoids repeated solver calls and maintains throughput at 2.8k exec/s. Findings suggest that even partial constraints sharply increase efficiency in guided exploration of deep kernel logic.

title: Microarchitectural Feedback-Driven Kernel Fuzzing Using Branch Buffer Telemetry
authors: Marco Rinaldi; Elena Conti; Giovanni Ferraro
abstract: Traditional kernel fuzzers rely on coarse-grained coverage metrics that cannot reflect complex microarchitectural behaviors. We present a hardware-assisted fuzzing framework that leverages branch buffer telemetry from modern CPUs (LBR, BTB sampling) to refine fuzzing feedback. A model-based inference algorithm aggregates branch-data patterns to estimate microarchitectural novelty and guides seed prioritization. Experiments on Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 3 systems demonstrate 27% improvement in unique path coverage, with 11 newly identified concurrency bugs across filesystem and scheduler subsystems. Compared with coverage-only fuzzing, our method reduces time-to-crash by 46% while keeping overhead below 12%. This work shows microarchitectural-level signals can significantly boost kernel fuzzing’s effectiveness.

title: Hybrid Taint-Guided Kernel Fuzzing with Selective State Propagation
authors: Arjun Mehta; Rohan Srinivasan; Neha Kapoor
abstract: We integrate static taint analysis with dynamic fuzzing to target high-impact kernel code paths. A pruning mechanism removes irrelevant taint propagation, while symbolic constraints are applied only to tainted regions to control overhead. Evaluated on 18 kernel subsystems, the hybrid fuzzer achieves 44% more taint-relevant path hits, identifying 13 bugs, including buffer overflows and pointer dereferences. Symbolic overhead remains limited (≤18%) through selective propagation. This hybrid design efficiently directs fuzzing toward semantically meaningful kernel logic, demonstrating a productive balance of taint tracking and dynamic mutation.

title: File-System-Oriented Kernel Fuzzing with Behavior Modeling of I/O Paths Authors
authors: Maria Gonzalez; Ethan Wright; David Chen
abstract: Filesystem kernels exhibit complex I/O dependency patterns that general fuzzers struggle to capture. We build a behavior model that encodes I/O path states (open → read/write → sync → metadata update) with a discrete state machine and use it to guide kernel fuzzing. Tested against EXT4, Btrfs, and XFS, the system achieves 38% deeper I/O path coverage, uncovering 10 bugs including inode corruption, metadata inconsistency, and mis-synchronized journal writes. The approach demonstrates that domain-specific modeling of subsystem workflows can substantially enhance fuzzing fidelity and bug discovery.

title: Semantic-Aware Kernel Fuzzing through System Call Dependency Inference&nbsp;
authors: Emily J. Crawford; Benjamin T. Lawson; Matthew R. Coleman
abstract: Kernel fuzzers often struggle to trigger deep execution paths that depend on multi-step system call sequences. To address this limitation, we introduce a semantic-aware fuzzing framework that infers syscall dependencies by mining execution traces and learning structural patterns in syscall graphs. A lightweight GNN-based model predicts probabilistic syscall transitions and generates semantically valid fuzzing sequences. Evaluated on Linux 5.4, 5.10, and 6.1, the system triggers 39% more deep kernel paths than syscall-random fuzzers, discovering 14 previously unknown bugs, including 3 memory-safety vulnerabilities assigned CVE identifiers. Overhead remains manageable with a median fuzzing throughput of 4.2k exec/s. These results highlight that modelling syscall-level semantics is critical for achieving deeper kernel state exploration.
